splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions must be finalized for calculating employer withdrawal liability from multiemployer pension plans. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers, as the timing of assumption selection directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be selected no later than the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about the limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, allowing courts to revoke supervised release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding because no statute authorizes such tolling, and judicial creation of the doctrine exceeds courts' authority.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under Section 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive collateral attack. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than 2255(h) alone would impose. The split affects federal prisoners' ability to bring successive challenges to their convictions.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to § 2255 motions, meaning federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of showing newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether and under what circumstances candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome could fundamentally reshape how courts evaluate candidate standing to challenge election rules, affecting mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge state election laws that allegedly dilute lawful votes or alter election procedures, based on competitive injury.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing to challenge state election procedures pre-election absent a concrete and particularized injury beyond generalized grievances about election administration.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to the Sentencing Commission's interpretation of ambiguous Sentencing Guidelines provisions in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should apply the rule of lenity or defer to the Sentencing Commission's commentary when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions in criminal sentencing. At least three circuits hold that lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit (and arguably others) have held that agency deference prevails. The issue has gained urgency after the Supreme Court overruled Chevron in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency interpretations in criminal sentencing contexts, resolving ambiguity in favor of the defendant.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference (Auer/Kisor or Stinson deference) to the Sentencing Commission's commentary prevails over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (requiring only one criterion to disqualify).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision. This governs whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums, and leads to vastly different outcomes for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on where they are prosecuted.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), meaning the word 'and' is read conjunctively.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion suffices
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is disqualifying from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' or as distributive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) encompasses inchoate offenses like conspiracy, as stated in Application Note 1, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes conspiracy and other inchoate offenses within the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation of the guideline or impermissibly expands its text. This split affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders under the Guidelines.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of § 4B1.2(b) that validly includes conspiracy and other inchoate offenses as controlled substance offenses for career offender purposes.

positions.label: Guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) is unambiguous and does not include inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its text and is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as a basis for compassionate release. Some circuits categorically prohibit such consideration, while others allow it as one factor among several. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this by authorizing consideration of unusually long sentences resulting from law changes, but at least one circuit has held the amendment exceeds the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law may be considered as one factor contributing to extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, either alone or in combination with other factors.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law cannot constitute or contribute to extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, as this would circumvent Congress's decision not to make such changes retroactive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) when the state criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally controlled or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies. This affects career offender designations and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions involving substances not on federal schedules.

positions.label: State offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include any state law drug offense, without requiring the substance to be federally controlled, because there is no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation onto the career offender guideline.

positions.label: State offense must involve federally controlled substance
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the underlying substance is also controlled under federal law, applying the categorical approach.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when converting in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the Chapter 13 petition filing and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This has significant consequences for debtors who convert in good faith but whose property has increased in value during the Chapter 13 case.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity inure to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, based on the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion property appreciation belongs to the debtor, consistent with the statutory structure and legislative history of § 348(f), which was designed to protect good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must challenge Bureau of Prisons decisions about conditions or circumstances of confinement (such as earned time credits or prerelease custody) exclusively through habeas corpus, or whether civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens) are also available.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions that affect the circumstances of confinement but do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment. This affects prisoners challenging BOP implementation of First Step Act programs, earned time credits, and transfer decisions.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the execution of a sentence, including prerelease custody and earned time credits, must be brought exclusively under habeas corpus.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights or other non-habeas actions to challenge BOP conditions and decisions that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of confinement.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Carmona v. United States Bureau of Prisons

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the violation of supervised release conditions when revoking supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to the purposes of supervised release itself.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether district courts at revocation hearings may impose sentences that punish defendants for violations of supervised release. Some circuits permit courts to expressly punish defendants at revocation, while others hold that the purpose of revocation sentences is limited to addressing the breach of trust and promoting future compliance.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations when imposing revocation sentences, placing the Sixth Circuit at the extreme end of this split.

positions.label: Punishment is not the purpose of revocation
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should focus on the breach of trust and the defendant's need for correctional treatment, not on punishing the defendant for the underlying violation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal deadline for filing a notice of appeal applies to a district court's order denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or a criminal matter (subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but acknowledged a lopsided circuit split on the issue.

positions.label: Civil appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and thus the 30-day civil deadline for filing a notice of appeal under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment order is part of the criminal case and therefore subject to the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting or enforcing laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any motor carrier... with respect to the transportation of property,' extends to preempt state negligence claims against freight brokers for negligently selecting or monitoring motor carriers.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that the FAAAA preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers because such claims relate to the brokers' services with respect to the transportation of property.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers for negligently hiring or supervising motor carriers are not preempted because they do not relate to the broker's prices, routes, or services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions can be used to address claims that overlap with habeas corpus relief under § 2255, such as claims of legal error in the original conviction or sentence. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors as part of the totality of circumstances, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider factors related to potential errors in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use § 3582 as habeas substitute
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot serve as a substitute for habeas corpus relief, and claims about legal errors in the underlying conviction or sentence are not cognizable as extraordinary and compelling reasons.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of racial discrimination in the operation of hotels and hospitality establishments under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 and related civil rights statutes?
splits.description: The Second Circuit's approach to evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality settings was found sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant Supreme Court review, suggesting a circuit split on the standards for proving discrimination liability and available remedies in service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that plaintiffs may establish discrimination claims under § 1981 in hospitality settings with less direct evidence of discriminatory intent, allowing broader theories of liability.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that discrimination claims in hospitality settings require more direct evidence of discriminatory intent and applies more restrictive standards for establishing liability.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Post-Bruen, circuits have split on whether the federal ban on firearm possession by unlawful drug users passes constitutional muster under the Second Amendment's historical-tradition test. Some circuits have upheld § 922(g)(3) as consistent with historical traditions of disarming dangerous persons, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of disarming those who pose a danger to themselves or others, and survives Second Amendment scrutiny even as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government cannot identify a sufficient historical tradition of disarming persons solely for drug use.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the Section 1 exemption for transportation workers, particularly whether last-mile delivery workers who distribute goods to retail stores are 'engaged in . . . interstate commerce.' This affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a wide range of distribution workers.

positions.label: Broad exemption — last-mile delivery workers qualify
positions.summary: Holds that workers who are part of a continuous interstate transportation chain, including those making last-mile deliveries of goods that have moved in interstate commerce, qualify as transportation workers exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow exemption — last-mile distributors do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that distribution workers delivering goods locally to retail stores are not 'transportation workers engaged in . . . interstate commerce' under Section 1 because they are not themselves moving goods across state lines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claims are based on labeling that the EPA approved. This affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticides nationwide.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would require labeling different from or in addition to what the EPA has approved.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because they impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements, consistent with the Supreme Court's Bates v. Dow Agrosciences framework.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
